990.dq: La palabra fonológica es una unidad de ritmo independiente compuesto de un mínimo de dos sílabas. ... El núcleo de una palabra básica se marca con un acento principal en la sílaba [contrasted with sec. 1] La frase fonológica se compone de una o más palabras fonológicas con un solo núcleo. 990.prule: Two-level phonemic tone (H vs unmarked L), lexically free (4 tone patterns on disyllables, 8 on trisyllables). The word has an 'acento principal' (núcleo) whose position is read off the tone pattern: on the H syllable if the word has a single H; on the first syllable if all syllables are L; on the first of a contiguous run of H syllables; 'complex' words with non-contiguous H syllables carry a nucleus on each H. No syllable-count or weight rule.
990.srule: Non-nuclear syllables of a basic word carry weaker accents: a slight controlled crescendo over the prenuclear syllables toward the nucleus and a slight controlled decrescendo after it (graded contour, no discrete rhythmic secondary-stress position). 'Complex' words (non-contiguous H syllables) carry a nucleus on each H syllable, not ranked as primary vs secondary.

990.exq_: El núcleo está: a) en la sílaba con tono alto cuando la palabra tiene sólo un tono alto, b) en la primera sílaba cuando todas las sílabas de la palabra tienen tono bajo, y c) en la primera sílaba de una serie cuando dos o más sílabas con tono alto de la palabra se presentan contiguas.
990.tone: Source treats tone and nasalization as the only suprasegmental phonemes ('Los rasgos suprasegmentales son el tono y la nasalización'); word accent (núcleo, 'acento principal') is described but is fully predictable from the lexical H/L tone pattern (falls on the first H; initial only when the word is all-L), so stress is parasitic on tone, not an independent positional rule. Mid tone is an allotone of H conditioned by position relative to the phrase nucleus.

991.prule: Word stress (breath force), independent of the high tone / pitch accent, falls on the stem syllable = the final syllable of every grammatical word that is not an enclitic; enclitics are bound into the preceding phonological word and never take the stress, so within the phonological word the stress position is not computable from syllable count (Story calls it 'phonemic... unpredictable' phonologically but 'predictable in grammatical terms'). No vowel-length/weight conditioning ('Nor is it necessary to draw a distinction between short and long vowels in order to predict stress as in Babine'). Coexisting culminative pitch-accent/tone system: each word in isolation carries one and only one H ('accent') on any syllable (lexical H, or default H at the right edge of the stem), downstep after a nonfinal H, all preceding syllables high, and tone perturbations between juxtaposed words by grammatical class (Story 1989:100-104, Nak'azdli speaker Francesca Antoine).
991.srule: Not mentioned in Story 1989 (sec. 1-2, pp. 100-104; chapter pp. 99-144): one breath-force stress per non-enclitic grammatical word on the stem (final) syllable is described, nothing on secondary or rhythmic stress; the 'one and only one accent' per word (p. 100) is the H pitch accent, not a stress count.

991.tone: Story 1989 (primary, read): Central Carrier is 'on the border between a language characterized by accent and one characterized by tone'; a word in isolation 'carries one and only one accent' (H); two word types -- H on a nonfinal syllable with a sharp 'downstep' to the next syllable, or H on the final syllable -- with every syllable before the H also high; disyllabic nouns sort into 2 sets and trisyllabic nouns into 3 by H location (any syllable may carry it); juxtaposed words undergo tone perturbations by grammatical class, 'much more characteristic of a tone language'; the stress (breath force) is explicitly 'independent of high tone (pitch accent)'. Pike 1986 (same speaker; via Gessner 2003:103-104) likens the step-down vs final-H contrast to Japanese and adds lowering/non-lowering tone sandhi; Poser 1992 (via Gessner 2003:105) likewise says stress and pitch accent coexist; toneless words get a default H at the right edge of the stem (Story per Gessner 2003:123). Walker 1979 (via Gessner 2003:102) instead describes 'two contrastive tones, high and low' with HH, LH, HL, LL all attested on bisyllables, says stress 'is not significant on the word level', and finds stress only as the peak high tone of a 'phonological pause group'. Cook 1976 called it 'lexical accent'; Morice 1932 saw only vestigial pitch contrasts; Krauss 1979 called Carrier tone one of 'the most difficult remaining mysteries of Athabaskan surface phonology'. The Wikipedia 'Japanese-like pitch accent'…

variants.prule: Stress, realized as increased vowel duration, falls on the verb-stem syllable (and on the stem syllable of deverbal nouns); it is the head of an obligatory uneven light-heavy iamb aligned with the right edge of the stem. Since the only verbal suffixes are relativizing suffixes, the stem is normally the last syllable of the word. An independent tone system (H phonologically active, culminative, partly lexical) supplies pitch prominence elsewhere in the word; underived mono- and bisyllabic nouns show pitch prominence only, with no durational stress.
variants.quote: [p.ii] One of the findings is that in addition to word-final stress in verbs, manifested primarily in terms of duration, "prominence" in the form of increased pitch is typically also found on one of the earlier syllables in the word. The location of the latter is partly determined phonologically, and in part lexically; certain prefixes appear to carry lexical tone ... [p.27] The stem, therefore, is always the last syllable in the word, unless there are any relativizing suffixes present. ... [p.51] For Dakelh, I will argue that verb stem syllable is stressed. This stress is realized by increased duration. ... [p.182] First of all, Dakelh does indeed seem to have both stress and tone, which appear to operate independently of each other. Stress is manifested as increased duration, and can be observed on verb stem syllables. As was argued in chapter 2, this is the head syllable of an obligatory uneven iamb (a bisyllabic light-heavy sequence), aligned with the right edge of the stem. Tone, which is entirely independent of this stress, is manifested by raised pitch. ... Every word appears to have at least one high-toned syllable (but see chapter 4 for systematic exceptions). All monosyllabic words (nouns) therefore have high tone. In bisyllabic nouns the location of high tone appears to be contrastive. Verbs, and deverbal nouns, generally have tone on their first or second syllable.

993.prule: Nouns and adjectives: stress on the final syllable of the base word (enclitics such as indefinite -èk unstressed; the definite suffix -aká is stressed). Verbs: stress assigned by a morphological hierarchy -- negative prefix na-/nâ- > preverb (war-, hał-, dâ-) > modal prefix (d)a-/bi- > otherwise final syllable of the verb stem (personal endings unstressed); infinitive stressed on its final syllable.
993.srule: Secondary stress on every other syllable counting leftward from the word-final primary stress, regardless of syllable weight (Hamid 2016: (na.ˌχoʃ)(χɑ.ˈna) 'hospital', (bɑ.ˌzɨɾ)(gɑ.ˈni) 'commercial', (ˌʃɑ)(ɾɨs.ˌtɑ)(ne.ˌti)(ja.ˈkɑn) 'the civilisations'); McCarus 1958 p. 34 likewise puts 'medium stress' on the pre-pretonic (or, when the primary is non-final, the post-posttonic) syllable. Not mentioned in Thackston 2006 (Stress, pp. 3-4).

evidence_works.detail: A sketch of Yerwa Kanuri by the author of the 1981 reference grammar that the entry already cites. It marks high tone with the acute accent and some falling tones with the circumflex and leaves low tone unmarked ('Tone is not indicated in the SKO. For the purposes of this introduction, we have included only the high tone (marked by the acute accent) marks and some falling tones marked by the circumflex. Syllables without tone markings are low tones.', p. 6 fn. 2), lists tone change among the word-derivation processes (pp. 15-16; 'The morphological processes which operate in the derivation of words include affixation, tone change, epenthesis, and reduplication.', with the pair Kanuri (high on the second syllable) 'person/people' vs Kanuri (high on the last syllable) 'language/adjective') and forms a noun plural by changing tone plus a high-tone suffix -wa ('The plural of the noun is formed through changing its tone and applying the high tone plural suffix always written as -wa (SKO).', pp. 9-10; the sentence starts on p. 9 and ends on p. 10). The dialect line in the row's quote ('speak a different dialect, differing especially as to tones', pp. 1-2) is a block quotation from Lukas (1937) that Hutchison reproduces, not his own observation. The word 'stress' does not occur in the text. Same author, same variety and same prosodic type as the entry's source; it adds nothing that changes kind, rule or sec_status.

evidence_works.work: Koelle 1854, Grammar of the Bornu or Kanuri Language (London: Church Missionary House: pp. 10, 13, 85, 274-275)
evidence_works.detail: Pre-phonemic missionary grammar based on one Kanuri speaker in Sierra Leone (preface p. viii: 'The only thing in which I found him a little uncertain, was the quantity of the vowels and the accent'). It marks a per-word 'accent' with the acute ('The accented syllable is indicated by the acute accent', p. 13 §9), places it on the second vowel of a diphthong ('When they receive the accent, it is always placed on the last of the two vowels, as in Greek', p. 10 §7), and describes morphological accent: 'The negative mood has always a strong accent on its last syllable, so that all the words are doubly accented' (p. 85) and, of the interrogative suffix, 'This suffix is generally marked out by a very strong accent when preceded by several unaccented syllables; but if the latter is not the case it is toneless' (p. 274 §274), 'Sometimes the suffix is altogether omitted, so that the interrogation is expressed by the tone only' (p. 275 §275). No positional stress rule is given; Koelle himself calls the unaccented state 'toneless' and the same marking 'tone', and read against Hutchison 1981 (two-tone language, compounding marked by tone change 'rather than by stress or accent change') his accent is the notation for high tone. The entry's cfw already records this reading; this item names the work formally.

998.qtr: In this paper, where necessary, flat-type accent is written 0 and falling-type accent (1). In the Tokyo dialect the position of the fall is distinctive and, as the number of moras grows, the accent types grow as n+1 (a word of n syllables has n+1 accent types), but in the Shuri dialect the position of the accent is fixed and non-distinctive. In this respect it resembles the Kagoshima dialect, likewise called a two-pattern word-tone dialect. The differences are that in Kagoshima the falling-type accent is on the second mora from the end whereas in Shuri it is on the second mora from the beginn…
998.dq: 首里方言は下降型と平板型の２型を区別する語声調方言である [Shuri is a word-tone (語声調) dialect distinguishing two types, falling and flat]; 首里方言ではアクセントの位置は決まっており非弁別的である [in Shuri the position of the accent is fixed and non-distinctive].
998.dloc: Nagano-Madsen & Karimata 2010, section 2 '琉球方言のアクセント', p.176 (main quote); p.184-185 (second passage); Nagano-Madsen 2011 p.1434 (English supporting quote in notes)
998.prule: Two-pattern lexical word-tone (pitch-accent) system: every word is either flat/平板型 (all moras level, 'unaccented') or falling/下降型 ('accented'); which class a word belongs to is lexical. Within the falling class the locus of the pitch fall is fixed and non-distinctive: after the 2nd mora from the beginning of the word (after the 1st mora in 2-mora words). The great majority of words are flat-type. No stress rule is described; prominence is pitch (F0) only.
998.quote: 本稿では必要に応じて平板型アクセントを0、下降型アクセントを⑴で表す。東京方言では下降の位置が弁別的であり、拍数が増えるとアクセントの型もｎ＋１（ｎ音節の語にはｎ＋１のアクセント型がある）のように増加するが、首里方言ではアクセントの位置は決まっており非弁別的である。この点、同じく２型の語声調方言といわれる鹿児島方言と似ている。異なるのは、鹿児島方言では下降型のアクセントが最後から２拍目であるのに対し、首里方言は最初から２拍目（ただし２拍語のときは１拍目）、また鹿児島方言の平板型は最後の拍が高いが、首里方言は通常、全部の拍が平らとされているなどの点である。なお、首里方言における下降型アクセントの占める割合は、東京方言や大阪方言のそれと比較すると極めて少なく、圧倒的多数の語が平板型アクセントである。 ... 首里方言は下降型と平板型の２型を区別する語声調方言であるので、（第２モーラの後に）ピッチの下降がある「荒儲けですか」と平板型「山田さんですか」を例文として使用した。

999.dq: Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word, i.e., a preferred rhythm of weak-strong, in which the weak position may only be filled by a short vowel.
999.dloc: Valentine 1996, section 'STRESS', pp. 312-314 (of the ALGQP PDF); bibliography entry for Rhodes 1976
999.heavy: long vowels: 'the weak position may only be filled by a short vowel' (long-vowel syllables cannot be foot-dependents and are always strong)
999.dflt: all-short-vowel words: weak-strong alternation from the left edge (2nd, 4th... syllables strong), final syllable 'often analyzed as extrametrical'; primary-stress locus unstated. Valentine adds that 'some dialects, notably those in northern Ontario, show stress shifts in sequences of short vowels', exemplified with a Severn Ojibwe speaker -- applicability to Central Ojibwa not stated.
999.prule: Pan-Ojibwe statement (Valentine 1996; no Central-Ojibwa-specific description reached): 'quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word', a weak-strong rhythm in which 'the weak position may only be filled by a short vowel' (so a long-vowel syllable can never be the weak member of a foot and is always a foot head); 'The final syllable is often analyzed as extrametrical' (Valentine's wording; the source does NOT say the final syllable is always strong -- that is the compilation Wikipedia summary after Valentine 2001 on Nishnaabemwin, unverified for this language). Which foot head carries PRIMARY word stress is not stated in this source.
999.srule: Valentine 1996 (pan-Ojibwe; nothing Central-Ojibwa-specific) gives one undifferentiated iterative parse rather than a separate secondary-stress rule: iambic (weak-strong) feet built left-to-right across the word, weak slot only a short vowel, so every foot head -- the 2nd of each pair of short-vowel syllables and every long-vowel syllable -- is metrically strong; his 'Metrically Structured Wordlist' foots words exhaustively (e.g. SS-SS-S mazinahigan). 1000.prule: Stress falls on the first syllable of the radical (root/stem): 'siempre se acentúa la primer sílaba del radical' (Knapp 2008:95, endorsed as 'descriptivamente correcta' by Arellanes & Romero 2021). The root syllable heads a syllabic trochee that is the minimal phonological word; suffixes and epenthetic vowels fill the weak branch, proclitics precede the tonic root syllable and enclitics stay outside the main foot. Equivalent to phonological-word-initial stress, since the p-word begins at the root.
1000.srule: Secondary (non-primary) prominences arise only from clitic strings and are placed by constituency, not by syllable count: two enclitics after the main root-headed trochee form an additional head-initial foot inside the phonological word, with secondary stress on the first enclitic (e.g. [ɾí.<(ˈʔêː.ɲé).(ˌkʰɔ̀.já)>] 'ya juego'); two proclitics form a head-initial foot outside the phonological word within the clitic group, with secondary stress on the first proclitic (e.g. [(ˌnù.ín).<(ˈʣùː.mɨ́).(ˌkʰɔ̀.ɓé).nú>] 'nuestra casa'); a lone proclitic or enclitic, or a third enclitic, stays unfooted and unstressed. A root with its suffix or epenthetic vowel carries the single main stress.

1000.tone: Tonal language: 'En términos fonológicos, cuenta con cuatro tonos: alto (á), bajo (à), descendente (â) y ascendente (ǎ)' (Antonio Victoria & Hernández Peña 2025). Lexical tone contrast sits on the stressed root-initial syllable; the post-tonic syllable of a simple radical has predictable tone (low, or high after a rising tone); compounds and loans have unpredictable tone on non-initial syllables but are still transcribed with initial stress. tn.quote: Finalmente, el mazahua cuenta con tres patrones tonales con valor fonológico: alto (A), bajo (B) y descendente (AB) (Pike 1951: 37; Amador 1976: 8; Romero 2017). Estos patrones tonales son contrastivos en las raíces; en cambio, las vocales epentéticas reciben un tono A ... es un tono flotante que marca el linde final de cada pie dentro de la palabra fonológica ... los sufijos y los enclíticos carecen de especificación tonal, mientras que los proclíticos sí tienen un tono propio, el cual puede ser A o B, pero no AB a diferencia de lo que ocurre con las raíces.
tn.translation: Finally, Mazahua has three tonal patterns with phonological value: high (A), low (B) and falling (AB) (Pike 1951: 37; Amador 1976: 8; Romero 2017). These tonal patterns are contrastive in roots; epenthetic vowels, by contrast, receive an A [high] tone ... it is a floating tone that marks the final boundary of each foot within the phonological word ... suffixes and enclitics lack tonal specification, whereas proclitics do have a tone of their own, which may be A or B, but not AB, unlike what happens with roots.

1001.prule: Primary word stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive, position unpredictable) but confined to a right-edge three-syllable window: it falls on one of the last three syllables of the word (final, penult, or antepenult). Minimal pairs by stress position abound (gayáŋ/gáyaŋ, ʔirít/ʔírit, bawí/báwi...). Stressed open penults/antepenults are lengthened (allophone 2); stressed closed syllables and open finals are not (allophone 1).
1001.srule: Secondary stress is non-phonemic and predictable from the primary: it falls on the first of the two syllables preceding the primary stress (two syllables before it) and on the second of the two syllables following it (two syllables after it), within the word; weaker volume/pitch rise than the primary, slight lengthening in open syllables. E.g. ninbàbʔaríka 'you deceived me', ʔamʔàmmaʔéna 'he is making it', domákarkà 'you go outside'.

A mid tone is often perceived, but no contrast is found at the lexical level. … a downstep rule lowers a high tone (i.e. ꜜH) when a low tone intervenes between two high tones, e.g. dʊ̃́ʊ̃̀ (sg. 1004.quote: El acento de intensidad tiene relevancia fonológica, ya que existe algún par mínimo sólo distinguido por su posición: ára ‘brillo’, ‘brillar’ ¹ ará ‘dar’ El acento puede caer en una de las dos últimas sílabas hacia la derecha, generalmente en la última. 1007.prule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word ROOT, regardless of word class and quantity-insensitive (predominantly open syllables). 1008.heavy: (for the superhigh accent only: long vowels; 'Superhigh accent is found only on a long vowel')
1008.dflt: (superhigh accent: high tone H4 on the first syllable of the word when no long vowel)
1008.prule: Tone language: six surface pitch patterns per syllable (low, high, low-high, high-low, lowfall, superhigh) organised into four contrastive tones (low, high, lowfall, superhigh); high tone has several sources (glottal stop H1, stem-final mora H2, pre-pronominal prefix iambic accent H3). The superhigh accent is morphosyntactically conditioned (subordinate verbs, deverbal nouns, adjectives), culminative, and placed by a default-to-opposite rule: 'Assign a superhigh accent to the last non-final long vowel of the word'; in the absence of a long vowel a high tone (H4) is assigned to the first syllable. Author explicitly states it is not a stress-accent system (violates Obligatoriness).
1008.srule: None: 'the superhigh accent is restricted to one per word... there is no ‘secondary’ superhigh accent... Only one H3 is allowed... there is no ‘secondary’ H3' (both accents culminative and non-obligatory; no rhythmic or secondary stress described).

1008.tone: Uchihara: Cherokee is 'the only [Iroquoian] language with a clear tonal system'; four contrastive tones with mora/syllable TBUs, OCP, floating tones, spreading. The superhigh 'accent' is culminative and predictable (last non-final long vowel, else initial H4 = default-to-opposite, unbounded QS trochee from the right) but NOT obligatory - it appears only in certain morphosyntactic categories - so the author classifies the system as neither canonical tone nor stress-accent but a combination; earlier literature (Lindsey 1987, Johnson 2005) called it pitch-accent. No word-stress rule independent of tone is described.

evidence_works.detail: Reference grammar built on the author's own recorded elicitation sessions with three named Oklahoma consultants (p.22: 'a large part of this analysis rests on elicitation with native speakers from Oklahoma. These sessions were recorded on a digital recorder'), checked against Pulte and Feeling, Scancarelli and the UCLA papers. It labels the system 'pitch accent' explicitly following Lindsey 1987 (p.109: 'I accept his lead and thus use the term ‘pitch accent language’ rather than ‘tone language’'), which the entry already registers as the earlier pitch-accent analysis that Uchihara 2013 reanalyses. Its stress section (pp.103-104) adds the perceptual detail that the word-final vowel is 'stressed and generally has a high tone that is slightly higher than a normal high tone' (= Lindsey's upstep, p.58) and that 'The stress does not fall on the final vowel if there is a highfall tone elsewhere in the word' - the highfall being the grammatically restricted tone ('Main clause verbs never carry a highfall tone, but subordinate verbs and words derived from verbs almost always carry this tone', p.104), i.e. the same culminative, morphosyntactically conditioned prominence the entry codes as Uchihara's superhigh accent. No instrumental measurement; no secondary stress mentioned; one prominence per word; word domain.

1012.prule: Stress is treated as a (non-linear) phoneme: exactly one heavy (primary) stress per free form, marked with an acute in the phonemic transcription of every word; its position is not derived by any rule and varies across words of equal length (píǧin initial vs bilóŋ final; hwáfæšən initial), following the English etymon. Second members of compounds demote to intermediate stress; emphatic stress falls on 'the usually accented syllable'; words keep their stress in phrases.
1012.srule: None within the word: 'Heavy stress occurs on one syllable of every free form; the other syllables have light stress' (Hall 1944 sec. 1.1). Hall's 'intermediate' stress is not a rhythmic secondary stress: it occurs only on the second member of a compound, on the syllable that has heavy stress when the word is independent (ǧós-píǧin).

1013.dq: Stress on individual words in Chinuk Wawa is generally but by no means exclusively on the penultimate syllable
1013.dloc: Grant 2013 APiCS survey ch. 74, section 5 'Chinuk Wawa phonetics and phonology' (final paragraph); Robertson 2020 blog post, opening paragraphs and tally
1013.prule: Strong default: stress on the penultimate syllable (Grant) / first syllable (Robertson: ~95% of words) — equivalent for the disyllables that dominate the lexicon; not exceptionless and not computable from syllable count. A lexically defined stratum of French-origin nouns with fused article (la-, li-, le-) is mostly final-stressed, and about half of those show variable (initial ~ final) stress; the CTGR 2012 dictionary marks stress per word.
1013.srule: Deciding survey (Grant 2013, sec. 5, sec. 16) does not mention secondary stress. Robertson 2018 ('Zenk's Law', crediting Zenk's grammar notes in the CTGR 2012 dictionary pp. 380-381, not seen by us) states a tendency: words of more than two syllables carry secondary stress on every other syllable counted from the main stress (t’əmánəwàs, k’ílapày), and Robertson 2020 reads the initial+final marks on trisyllabic la-nouns (lákamás) as possibly this pattern. Jacobs 1932 p. 32 (first-hand, Victoria Howard) states the opposite: 'There is no secondary stress.'

1013.cfw: Jacobs 1932, Zenk 1993 and Zenk & Johnson 2004, all from first-hand work, together with Robertson's 2020 tally of the Grand Ronde dictionary, describe stress as fixed word by word with no rule that predicts it (most words initial, French loans final), and the only discrepancy is Grant 2013's survey wording that the default is penultimate rather than initial, which comes to the same thing in the two-syllable words that make up most of the lexicon.
